An architecture decision record (ADR) is a short note that captures one decision: why it was needed, what was chosen and what follows from it. Future maintainers should be able to read a record and understand the reasoning without asking the person who made it.
Write an ADR when a decision is hard to reverse, affects more than one system, or would puzzle a future reader. Do not write one for routine choices.

Each record lives in this folder as ADR-NNNN-short-title.md and has five sections: Status, Context, Decision, Consequences and Alternatives considered. Copy _template.md to begin. Status Meaning Proposed Written, under discussion Accepted In force Rejected Considered and declined Superseded Replaced by a later record, which it links to Records are never rewritten once accepted. Supersede them instead.

ADR Title Status ADR-0001 Docusaurus on GitHub Pages for the docs Accepted (retrospective) ADR-0002 Justify subdomains before creating them Proposed ADR-0003 Separate the public API from the webhook services Accepted (retrospective)

documents.s: ADR-0001: Docusaurus on GitHub Pages for the docs

documents.t: The ecosystem needs a documentation site at docs.rjmlaird.co.uk that supports versioned documentation, search, diagrams and a custom domain, and that is cheap to run for a single maintainer. The services themselves run on Cloudflare Workers, but documentation is static content.
Build the docs with Docusaurus (with Mermaid and local search enabled) and deploy them to GitHub Pages using GitHub Actions. The docs hostname points at GitHub Pages through a CNAME record.

Hosting is free and tied to the repository. Deployment is automatic on a push to main. Broken links fail the build, which protects the quality of the site. GitHub Pages cannot set custom response headers, which limits security headers. There are no pull-request preview deployments. DNS is split between GitHub Pages and Cloudflare, so the domain model must document both.
To confirm: which alternatives were weighed at the time (for example another static documentation framework, or hosting the docs on Cloudflare). They were not recorded.

The planning inventory lists 34 candidate subdomains, many of which overlap. Each real subdomain brings its own DNS record, certificate, deployment and navigation. Search authority is split across hostnames. Because the session cookie is shared across *.rjmlaird.co.uk, every subdomain also sits in the same trust zone.

Create a subdomain only if it needs at least one of: a different runtime or build, a different security boundary, a different owner or audience with a distinct brand, or an external platform that requires it. Otherwise deliver the content as a path on the main site. Every subdomain must have an entry in the subdomain catalogue with a status before a DNS record is added.

Around 16 of the inventory hostnames become paths, and 5 are not created. One certificate, one navigation and one deployment cover most content. Some short URLs (for example cv.rjmlaird.co.uk) are lost unless a vanity redirect is added. Moving a section to its own subdomain later is possible, but needs redirects.

One subdomain per topic (the original inventory). Rejected: heavy maintenance, fragmented authority, and a larger shared-cookie surface. No subdomains at all. Rejected: the Workers services, docs and private tools genuinely need separate hostnames.
Recorded retrospectively This reflects a design stated by the owner. Deployment of both systems is not yet verified.
documents.s: ADR-0003: Separate the public API from the webhook services

documents.t: Two kinds of service are needed. One serves public portfolio data to anyone. The other handles commercial events from Stripe, Cal.com and HubSpot, and updates customer records. They have different audiences, different security needs and very different consequences if compromised.

Keep them separate. The public portfolio API lives in rjmlaird-api at api.rjmlaird.co.uk. Commercial operations live in the private rjmlaird-services repository, with webhook ingress at hooks.rjmlaird.co.uk. The services repository exposes no public portfolio data and no customer lists.

A flaw in the public API cannot expose payment or CRM data, because it holds none. Each system can have its own rate limits, secrets and release cadence. There are two repositories and two hostnames to maintain. Shared concerns, such as sign-in, are handled by auth rather than duplicated.
One combined API. Rejected: it mixes public and private concerns and enlarges the blast radius of any fault.

Several parts of the ecosystem run without anyone pressing a button: a documentation build on every merge, queue consumers that react to payments and bookings, and a planned daily wiki sync. This page lists them and sets out how new automation should behave.

Workflow Trigger What it does Status Docs build and deploy Push to main; pull request build check Typechecks, builds and deploys the docs Live (repository) Stripe event processing Verified webhook, then queue Records payment events In development Cal.com event processing Verified webhook, then queue Records booking events In development HubSpot sync Queue consumer Updates the CRM; HubSpot stays authoritative In development Client-delivery follow-ups Queue consumer Triggers follow-up steps after a booking or payment In development Wiki sync Daily schedule Pulls the chosen Notion page tree into D1 Proposed (architecture agreed) Zotero research ingest Request to /v1/research Stores library data in R2 under papers/ In development Local scripts (data parsing, metadata extraction) Manual To confirm To confirm

These are proposed standards for any new automation: Verify before trusting. Check the sender's signature on every inbound webhook before doing any work. Acknowledge fast, process later. Accept the event, put it on a queue, return quickly. Do the work in a consumer. Be idempotent. The same event arriving twice must not charge, email or record twice. Store a processed-event key. Fail visibly. Failed messages should land somewhere you will see them, not disappear. One authority per record. Never synchronise in both directions. HubSpot owns contacts; the automation writes to it. Run on a schedule only if you must. Prefer manual or event-driven triggers for the first release. The wiki starts with a scheduled pull and no webhooks.

Do any local scripts run on the owner's machine (for example for Zotero or metadata extraction), and what do they depend on? What happens to a message that keeps failing: is there a dead-letter queue? Who is told when a scheduled job fails?

Astro suits a bespoke, design-led main site. Docusaurus provides navigation, versioning, search and Mermaid support for documentation without custom work.

Type-safe validation with Zod is used in the services code (the shared service contracts package, owner-stated). Whether the main site validates content with Astro content collections and Zod schemas is not yet documented. To confirm Whether the main site uses Astro content collections, and with which schemas. Whether the CV, portfolio and research content have a structured data format, or are ordinary pages. Where Zotero-derived research data is meant to surface on the site.

The main site's src/styles/global.css is the single source of truth for the brand: an ink, teal, amber and violet palette, with Space Grotesk, Inter and JetBrains Mono typography, designed to meet WCAG AA or better. The rjmlaird-dev project shares the same file. The docs site reproduces the brand in src/css/custom.css and loads the three fonts from Google Fonts. To confirm / technical debt The docs repository's README states that custom.css holds placeholder hex values to be copied by hand from global.css. Until that is done, the two sites do not match, and every future brand change needs a manual copy. Candidate fixes, in order of effort: Copy the values once and note the date here. Publish the tokens as a small package or a single hosted CSS file that both sites import. Generate both stylesheets from one tokens file. Also consider self-hosting the fonts. Loading them from Google Fonts makes a third-party request on every docs page view, which should be reflected in the privacy notice.
Write or edit Markdown (or MDX) on a branch. Preview locally with pnpm start. Open a pull request; CI typechecks and builds, failing on broken links. Merge to main; the site deploys.
Docusaurus parses .md files as MDX. Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose are read as code, so put them in backticks or a code block. This is the most common cause of a failed docs build.

The domain architecture of rjmlaird.co.uk is intended to keep DNS small, predictable and easy to audit. This page records what is known about the current setup, what is inferred, and the rules that decide whether a new subdomain gets created. Status: Draft Only the docs hostname is verified from a repository. The registrar and authoritative nameservers are not yet documented. Treat everything marked inferred or To confirm as unchecked.

Question Answer Basis Who is the registrar? To confirm Not recorded Who runs the authoritative nameservers? Probably Cloudflare Inferred: the auth Worker uses a Custom Domain route, which requires the zone's DNS to be managed by Cloudflare How does docs resolve? CNAME to GitHub Pages Repository README and static/CNAME How do Worker hostnames resolve? Cloudflare Worker Custom Domains Owner-stated for auth and hooks Is there a wildcard DNS record? To confirm Not recorded Is DNSSEC enabled? To confirm Not recorded The practical consequence is a split hosting model. Static content may live on GitHub Pages or another static host, while services live on Cloudflare Workers. DNS is the one place that holds the whole picture together, which is why it deserves its own documentation.

The planning inventory names www.rjmlaird.co.uk as the canonical web presence and rjmlaird.co.uk as the root domain. Proposed rule: pick one canonical host and permanently redirect (301) the other to it. Following the inventory, that means: https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk serves the site. https://rjmlaird.co.uk redirects to https://www.rjmlaird.co.uk, preserving the path. Trade-offs. Using www as canonical is the traditional choice and keeps the apex record simple. Using the apex as canonical gives shorter URLs and matches how the site is already referred to elsewhere. Either works; what matters is choosing one and applying it everywhere, including sitemaps, rel="canonical" tags and cookie scope. To confirm / technical debt The docs site currently links to the apex (https://rjmlaird.co.uk) in its navbar and footer, which contradicts the inventory's choice of www as canonical. Decide which host is canonical, then update docusaurus.config.ts to match. Record the decision in an ADR.

Lowercase, single-label, one purpose. For example docs, never docs-and-guides. Names describe a function, not a vendor. No subdomain without a catalogue entry. Every record must correspond to a row in the subdomain catalogue with a status and an owner. No wildcard DNS record. A wildcard hides typos and widens the takeover surface. (The shared session cookie is scoped to *.rjmlaird.co.uk, but that is a cookie setting, not a DNS record.) Remove records when retiring a service. A CNAME pointing at a deleted GitHub Pages site or an abandoned SaaS tenant can be claimed by someone else. Delete the DNS record in the same change that retires the service. Prefer redirects to new hostnames. A retired subdomain should redirect to its path replacement for as long as old links are likely to exist, then be removed.

Pattern Used by Status CNAME to a GitHub Pages hostname docs Live (per README; confirm in the DNS provider) Worker Custom Domain (record managed by Cloudflare) auth, hooks In development Worker Custom Domain api, wiki Proposed Apex and www Main site Live; host to confirm CNAME to an external SaaS Possibly newsletter, booking Deferred; depends on provider support

Changes to the rjmlaird.co.uk ecosystem flow from a local machine, through an automated check, to production. This page documents the pipeline that is verified today (the docs site), the environment model planned for the Workers services, and the places where the two differ.

The docs repository uses pnpm, with the version pinned in package.json through packageManager (enable it with corepack enable). Node.js 20 or later is required locally. Local commands pnpm install pnpm start # live preview at http://localhost:3000 pnpm run build # production build; fails on broken links pnpm run typecheck # TypeScript check pnpm validate # typecheck plus build; what CI runs

The services repositories are pnpm workspace monorepos written in TypeScript. Wrangler runs Workers locally and deploys them; Vitest runs the tests. Exact local commands are To confirm and should be added to each repository's README.

The workflow is .github/workflows/ci.yml. Aspect Setting Triggers Push to main, any pull request, and manual dispatch Build job Checkout, pnpm setup, Node.js 22 with the pnpm cache, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile, then pnpm run validate Deploy job Runs only on a push to main, after the build job succeeds Hosting GitHub Pages through the official Pages actions, with the build directory as the artifact Permissions contents: read, pages: write, id-token: write Concurrency One run at a time in the pages group; in-progress runs are not cancelled Two settings make the pipeline strict by design: onBrokenLinks: 'throw' and onBrokenMarkdownLinks: 'throw'. A broken internal link therefore fails the build, and a failed build never reaches production. Broken anchors only warn.

The CI and deployment pipeline for the Workers repositories is not yet documented. The intended shape, based on the owner's plans, is Wrangler-based deployment per environment with tests run first. To confirm Whether Worker deployments run from GitHub Actions or from a local wrangler deploy, and which credentials they use.

Surface Environments Preview URLs Docs site One: production None. Pull requests run a build check, but nothing is deployed for review rjmlaird-services Development, staging, production (owner-stated plan) Staging serves as the preview Other Workers To confirm To confirm Main site To confirm To confirm Branching. The docs repository uses a single long-lived branch, main. Work happens on short-lived branches and reaches main through a pull request. Direct pushes to main also deploy, so protect the branch if more than one person contributes. Rollback. Revert the commit on main. The workflow redeploys the previous state. For Workers, redeploy the previous version with Wrangler, or use the platform's version history. Versioned docs. The documentation can be frozen at a release with pnpm run version:cut. The architecture section describes the current system, so decide whether it should be snapshotted along with product documentation (see the technical debt below).
Dotted lines are planned or unconfirmed.

The docs workflow uses no repository secrets. It relies on the built-in token and the Pages deployment permissions. Worker secrets are intended to live as Cloudflare Worker secrets, never in the repository. The wiki's Notion token is the stated example. Environment-specific values belong in Wrangler configuration per environment. Anything secret never does.

To confirm / technical debt Shallow checkout. The workflow uses the default actions/checkout@v4, which fetches only the latest commit. The docs show last-updated times (showLastUpdateTime: true), which are read from git history. With a shallow clone those times are likely to be wrong. Setting fetch-depth: 0 on the checkout step is the usual fix. Verify against the live site. Duplicate CNAME file. There is a CNAME at the repository root as well as static/CNAME. Only the one in static/ is copied into the build. Confirm the root copy is intentional. No preview deployments. Reviewing a docs change means running it locally. Actions pinned to major tags. Pinning to commit hashes is stricter, at the cost of manual updates. Versioning scope. Decide whether the architecture section is included in version:cut snapshots.

Fingerprinted files (a hash in the filename) can be cached for a long time and marked immutable. Unversioned files should have short cache lifetimes or revalidation. Private buckets (such as the Zotero store) must never share a bucket, a domain or caching rules with public assets.

Good observability for a small ecosystem means knowing quickly that something is broken, finding out why, and telling the right people. Almost none of that is documented as in place, so this page is mainly a proposal and a list of questions. Status: Proposed No monitoring, error-tracking, analytics or status tooling is confirmed. Candidate tools below are options to evaluate, not decisions.

Capability Status Build failure notification for the docs GitHub Actions run status only Worker logs and metrics Cloudflare provides these for Workers; whether and how they are used is to confirm Uptime monitoring To confirm Error tracking To confirm Public status page Proposed (status); no confirmed implementation Analytics To confirm

Each service should offer one cheap endpoint that returns whether it is healthy. The API template in these docs already sketches GET /status returning ok and version; adopt a consistent form such as GET /v1/status across every Worker.

Log events, not secrets or personal data. Include a request or event identifier so a failed webhook can be traced from provider to consumer. Keep retention short unless a legal or business reason says otherwise.
Host any public status page outside the infrastructure it reports on. A status page that goes down with the thing it monitors tells nobody anything.
Alert on a small number of things you would act on at once: webhook failures, a failed scheduled sync, and the public sites being unreachable. Too many alerts will be ignored.

A pragmatic process for a single maintainer: Detect. An alert, a failed workflow run or a report. Assess. What is affected, and is any personal data involved? Contain. Roll back, disable a route or rotate a secret. Communicate. Update the status page if public services are affected. If personal data may have been exposed, consider legal reporting duties promptly. Fix and verify. Review. Write a short note. If the cause was an architectural weakness, record an ADR.
Is any uptime monitoring running? Are Cloudflare Worker logs enabled, and where are they read? Who is notified when a scheduled job fails? Is there any analytics on the public sites, and if so which?

This section documents the architecture behind rjmlaird.co.uk: the sites, services and infrastructure that make up Ryan Laird's personal, professional and technical web presence. It is written for four readers: the owner and maintainer, future collaborators and contractors, technical readers who want to see how the pieces fit, and non-technical readers who only need a mental model. Read the status labels The subdomain list that this section is built around is a planning model, not an inventory of running services. Every site and service carries a status label, and anything not yet checked is marked To confirm. If a page does not say something is Live, do not assume it is.

Label Meaning Live Serving real traffic today. In development Being built; not yet serving production traffic. Proposed Designed or recommended, but no build has started. Deferred Deliberately postponed until there is a concrete need. Includes exploratory ideas. Not recommended Considered and advised against. Recorded so the question is not reopened by accident. Deprecated Was live; scheduled for removal or already retired.

Each page also carries a confidence value in its front matter: Verified (checked against a repository or configuration), Partly verified, or Unverified (from planning notes only). Where a statement is inferred rather than confirmed, it is flagged inline.

The ecosystem exists to do five jobs: Present a clear professional and personal brand. Publish writing, research and astronomy and space communication. Sell and schedule services such as tutoring, mentoring and coaching. Explore ideas in public through experiments and data pieces. Run a small amount of back-office automation behind the scenes. In scope: the public sites, the services and APIs, the documentation site and the infrastructure that connects them. Out of scope: the internals of third-party platforms (GitHub, Stripe, Cal.com, HubSpot, Notion, Zotero). Only the integration points are documented here.

Status before subdomain. Nothing gets a DNS record until it has a catalogue entry with a purpose, a status and an owner. Paths before subdomains. Content that shares a build, an audience and a security boundary belongs at a path on the main site. A subdomain must justify itself (see the subdomain catalogue). Static first. Use a static site wherever possible. Add a Worker only where server-side behaviour is genuinely needed. Keep public and private surfaces apart. The public portfolio API and the commercial webhook services are separate systems. Private tools sit behind authentication. One brand system. global.css on the main site is the single source of truth for the visual identity. Other sites copy from it, never the reverse. Say what we do not know. Unknowns are written down as To confirm, not papered over. Prefer reversible, low-cost choices. This is a one-person operation; every extra moving part is maintenance debt.

This table lists the surfaces with some evidence behind them. The full list, including purely planned subdomains, is in the subdomain catalogue. Think of the ecosystem as a shop with four areas: The shop windows are the public sites: the main site, the docs, the labs and, later, space and research content. Visitors browse them freely. The locked doors are the sign-in service and the private wiki. Only the owner gets through. The back office is the set of small services that receive a payment or a booking, record it and update the customer record, without anyone pressing a button. The filing cabinets are the databases and storage buckets where those services keep their records and files.

This page describes the controls that protect the ecosystem and the data it handles. It separates controls that are known from those that are proposed, and it highlights the places where the architecture makes a trade-off that readers should understand. Not a compliance statement This page documents intended design. It is not a security audit, and it is not legal advice. Anything marked To confirm has not been checked.

Zone Examples Who can reach it Status Public content Main site, docs, labs Anyone Live Public API api Anyone, with rate limits Proposed Machine-facing hooks Verified third-party senders only In development Authenticated wiki, any future tools Allow-listed GitHub accounts Proposed

Control Detail Status Sign-in GitHub OAuth through auth, restricted to an allow-list In development Private wiki Cloudflare Access, initially one account Proposed Webhooks Signature verification on every inbound request In development Public data hooks exposes no portfolio data or customer lists Owner-stated design

The design shares one session cookie across *.rjmlaird.co.uk. This gives single sign-on across the ecosystem, but it has a consequence that shapes other decisions: every subdomain is inside the same trust zone. Any page on any subdomain receives the cookie. Practical rules that follow: Never host untrusted or user-generated content on any subdomain. This is one reason to avoid upload and sandbox. Treat a compromise of any subdomain as a potential compromise of the session. Keep the number of subdomains small, and keep the cookie Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite-restricted. Prefer scoping cookies to the narrowest host that needs them wherever sign-in is not required. To confirm The cookie's exact attributes, its lifetime, and how an administrator is revoked from the allow-list.

Secrets are held as Cloudflare Worker secrets, not in repositories (the wiki's Notion token is the stated case). The docs workflow needs no custom secrets. Dependencies are installed with --frozen-lockfile in CI, so builds use exactly the versions committed. Not yet documented: secret rotation, who holds recovery access, and where API tokens for HubSpot, Stripe and Cal.com are stored. These belong here once confirmed.

Topic Position Transport security HTTPS everywhere; see Domain and DNS model Docs response headers GitHub Pages does not allow custom response headers, so a strict Content-Security-Policy or Permissions-Policy header cannot be set there. A meta tag can cover part of this. Worker response headers Can be set in code; standard set to be agreed Rate limiting Required for any public endpoint; mechanism to confirm Subdomain takeover Mitigated by deleting DNS records when a service is retired

The integrations in use process personal data: HubSpot (contacts), Stripe (payments), Cal.com (bookings) and the sign-in service (GitHub identity). The docs site also loads fonts from Google Fonts, which makes a third-party request from visitors' browsers. The following should be reflected in a single privacy page at /privacy on the main site and linked from every site's footer: What data each integration collects and why. Retention periods. How a person requests access to or deletion of their data. Which third parties act as processors. Whether any analytics or cookies are used.

Threat Mitigation Forged webhook Signature verification and idempotency Replayed webhook Store processed-event keys Leaked secret Worker secrets; never commit; rotate on suspicion Dangling DNS record Remove records with the service Compromised subdomain under shared cookie Few subdomains; no untrusted content Malicious dependency Lockfile; review updates

Are any analytics or error-tracking tools installed on any site? What are the allow-list and revocation procedures for auth? Are there security headers set on the main site? Is two-factor authentication enforced on GitHub, Cloudflare, the registrar and HubSpot?

Consistent names and consistent pages make a sprawling ecosystem easier to navigate. This page records the naming conventions already in use, and the standards every architecture page must follow.

Thing Convention Example Hostname Lowercase, one label, describes a function docs, auth, hooks Repository rjmlaird- followed by the purpose rjmlaird-docs, rjmlaird-auth, rjmlaird-services Worker service Matches the repository or the app rjmlaird-auth API routes Versioned prefix /v1/webhooks/stripe KV keys Versioned prefix per service auth:v1: Environments development, staging, production rjmlaird-services plan Monorepo layout apps/, workers/, packages/, migrations/, docs/ rjmlaird-services Documentation files Lowercase, hyphenated domain-model.md ADR files ADR-NNNN-short-title.md ADR-0001-docusaurus-on-github-pages.md

Use clear, precise British English: optimisation, centralised, programme. Use sentence case for headings. Keep one idea per page; link rather than repeat. Capitalise system names consistently: Cloudflare Workers, Astro, Docusaurus, Zod, GitHub Pages. Prefer plain language, but include the technical detail a maintainer needs.

Every architecture page uses this structure: Front matter (below). An introductory paragraph saying what the page covers. A status admonition if the page is not fully verified. Headings at ## and ### only. Tables or lists where they help; short paragraphs elsewhere. A To confirm section if anything is unverified. A Related pages list.

Front matter --- id: page-identifier title: Page title in sentence case description: One sentence for search results and link previews. sidebar_position: 1 status: Draft confidence: Partly verified last_reviewed: 2026-10-11 --- Field Values Notes status Live, In development, Proposed, Draft, Deferred, Deprecated The state of the page's subject. Use Draft for pages that mix several subjects, and give per-item status in tables confidence Verified, Partly verified, Unverified How much has been checked against a repository or configuration last_reviewed A date When a person last checked the content against reality ADRs are the exception: their status is Proposed, Accepted, Rejected or Superseded. The built-in "last updated" footer comes from Git history. last_reviewed is separate: it records when someone verified the page, not when it was last edited.
Labels are defined in the architecture overview. Use them in tables as plain text, with the evidence in brackets where it matters, for example "Live (repository)".

Use a note admonition with a fixed title, so they can be searched for: Uncertainty callout :::note[To confirm] What is unknown, and how to find out. ::: Technical debt callout :::note[To confirm / technical debt] What is missing or deferred, and the suggested fix. ::: Never fill a gap with a plausible guess. If a provider, record, tool or setting is unconfirmed, say so.
Curly braces and angle brackets in ordinary prose break the build because Docusaurus reads .md as MDX. Put them in backticks or a code block.

Record any decision that is hard to reverse, affects several systems, or would puzzle a future reader. Store records in docs/architecture/adrs/, named ADR-NNNN-short-title.md. Use the template at docs/architecture/adrs/_template.md (a file starting with an underscore is excluded from the site). Every record has these sections: Status, Context, Decision, Consequences and Alternatives considered. Status is one of Proposed, Accepted, Rejected or Superseded. Never rewrite an accepted record. Supersede it with a new one that links back. See the ADR index.

To prevent architectural drift, every hostname under rjmlaird.co.uk is registered here with a status, a purpose and a recommendation. This page is the definitive answer to the question "does this subdomain exist, and should it?" This is a planning model The original inventory contained 34 entries. Only a few of them are verified as live. A row being present in this catalogue does not mean the service is running. Check the Status column.

Status labels are defined in the architecture overview. The brackets after a status give the evidence behind it: Evidence Meaning Repository Verified from a repository's configuration Owner-stated Described by the owner, not independently checked Linked Referenced from another live site None Appears only in the planning inventory

Priority Meaning Now Needed for the current build or already live Next Worth doing once the current work lands Later Reasonable, but not before there is content or demand Defer Postpone until a concrete requirement appears Merge Do not create; deliver as a path on another site Avoid Do not create; adds complexity without enough benefit
Content, Application, Infrastructure, Tooling or Services (revenue-related pages).

A subdomain earns its place only if it needs at least one of the following: A different runtime or build, such as a Worker or a separate static generator. A different security boundary, such as private access or untrusted input. A different owner or audience with a genuinely separate brand. An external platform that requires it, such as a SaaS custom domain. Everything else becomes a path on the main site. Paths share one certificate, one set of search authority, one deployment and one navigation, so they are cheaper to run and better for search.

Applying the justification rule above to all 37 entries gives this end state: Outcome Hostnames Keep as subdomains www (with apex redirect), docs, labs, space, research, api, auth, hooks, wiki Add later if needed status, one asset host (cdn or similar) Defer dev, courses, dashboards, mcp Merge into paths cv, portfolio, astro, talks, tutoring, physics, maths, mentoring, coaching, resources, stem, booking, bio, newsletter, privacy, images Avoid home, sandbox, dam, upload, app

Criterion Effect of many subdomains Effect of paths Maintainability One build, deployment and navigation per subdomain One build and one navigation SEO Search authority is split across hostnames Authority accumulates on one host DNS and certificates A record, a certificate and a hosting target each Nothing extra Security boundary Every subdomain sits under the shared session cookie scope, so a weak or untrusted one weakens all of them Same boundary, but fewer surfaces Branding Visitors see a fragmented set of properties One coherent brand Long-term cost Each is a permanent maintenance liability Marginal

tutoring, physics, maths, mentoring and coaching share one audience and one booking flow. A single /services section with a page per offering, and one booking link, is easier to maintain and ranks better than five separate sites. resources already has a sanctioned path alternative in the inventory, and should take it.

research is kept because it may carry its own build and data pipeline. If it turns out to be an ordinary set of essays, merge it into /research. space is kept because it serves a distinct audience and can carry a distinct identity. If it never grows its own navigation, merge it too. labs is kept because experiments carry unpredictable dependencies that should not share a build with the main site.

A subdomain that only redirects (for example cv to /cv) is cheap to run but still needs a DNS record and a certificate. Create one only if the short address appears on printed or fixed material, and record it here.
